video_title: What’s up with heat-pump water heaters?
gist: Volts host David Roberts interviews Reservoir CEO Luke Winston Almansar on a software-driven heat pump water heater (about $4-6k installed, claims 80% less energy than resistance), covering the vertically integrated install model, VPP/demand-response potential, and policy headwinds from the ended IRA credit and threatened 2029 DOE standard.

themes.theme: US water heater market structure and economics

insights.claim: About 10 million water heaters are replaced per year in the US; ~45% burn gas (declining), ~50% are electric (rising), and only ~4% of electric units (about 2% of all sales) are heat pumps.
insights.speaker: David Roberts
insights.so_what: Heat pump share of a ~10M/yr replacement market is tiny, so the addressable runway is large.

insights.claim: Water heating is roughly 20% of home energy use, second only to space heating, and a conventional electric resistance water heater uses more electricity per year than an EV.
insights.speaker: David Roberts
insights.so_what: Under-discussed load sits in the decarbonization and grid-planning blind spot.

insights.claim: Heat pump water heaters have stayed ~2% of the market despite not being new technology (invented in the 1940s) because of cost and unreliability, and plumbers fear them and rarely stock them; Home Depot sometimes cannot supply them.
insights.speaker: Luke Winston Almansar (Reservoir CEO)
insights.so_what: Distribution and installer behavior, not technology, is the adoption bottleneck, favoring vertically integrated installers.

insights.claim: Roughly a third of Reservoir installs are emergency replacements; having stock and responding within 24 hours matters because failed water heaters are replaced with whatever is available.
insights.speaker: Luke Winston Almansar (Reservoir CEO)
insights.so_what: Replacement-driven market rewards availability and speed over efficiency marketing.

insights.claim: About half the country lacks gas access and ~90% of Florida water heaters are electric resistance; blue states have more gas and red states further south more electric, so efficiency standards and incentives bite unevenly.
insights.speaker: Luke Winston Almansar (Reservoir CEO)
insights.so_what: Southern and electric-only markets are the clearest economics for heat pump water heaters.

themes.theme: Reservoir product, cost and unit economics

insights.claim: Reservoir's 50-gallon unit uses a standard heat pump but adds an onboard computer that learns usage over about a month and pre-heats, claiming 30%+ more heat pump use (less resistance backup) and about $800-1,000/yr savings vs electric resistance, ~$100/yr vs a typical heat pump water heater.
insights.speaker: Luke Winston Almansar (Reservoir CEO)
insights.so_what: Value is software and integration on commodity components, so differentiation is thin on hardware but real on installed performance.

insights.claim: Reservoir prices at roughly $4,000-6,000 before incentives including install and removal (about $3,950 after Massachusetts incentives of ~$1,500 headline), versus $2,500-6,000+ for an electric resistance install and $5,000-10,000 for a tankless gas system in the Boston metro.
insights.speaker: Luke Winston Almansar (Reservoir CEO)
insights.so_what: Install labor, not hardware, dominates cost; integration that cuts install cost is the lever.

insights.claim: Versus gas tank heaters in Boston the savings are only a couple hundred dollars a year because natural gas is cheap, so the company says it needs predictive intelligence to beat gas on total cost.
insights.speaker: Luke Winston Almansar (Reservoir CEO)
insights.so_what: Gas is the hard competitor; economics depend on local gas vs electricity prices.

insights.claim: Reservoir is vertically integrated in design, install (licensed plumbing company in Massachusetts, coordinated electricians) and service but uses a contract manufacturer and commodity components, installs in one visit after a photo-based virtual assessment, and operates in MA, RI, ME and NH with a goal of 20-30 metros nationwide in 2-3 years.
insights.speaker: Luke Winston Almansar (Reservoir CEO)
insights.so_what: Service-led, install-owned model is the differentiator; scaling labor across metros is the execution risk.

insights.claim: Cold rooms and small closets reduce heat pump water heater efficiency: units work down to ~42 F before resistance backup kicks in, unfinished basements and garages are best, and the company does not recommend its unit for tiny apartment water heater closets.
insights.speaker: Luke Winston Almansar (Reservoir CEO)
insights.so_what: Housing stock matters: single-family homes with basements are the near-term target market.

insights.claim: Reservoir offers a 10-year parts warranty and 2-year labor warranty, plus an electric anode rod to prevent tank corrosion, which is the main failure mode of conventional tanks, and monitors compressor temperature and leaks remotely.
insights.speaker: Luke Winston Almansar (Reservoir CEO)
insights.so_what: Durability and monitoring address the main reliability objection; warranty labor term is short relative to parts.

themes.theme: Grid flexibility and virtual power plants

insights.claim: Water heaters are a long-promised distributed energy resource, but VPP efforts stalled because devices are not connected: weak hardware-software execution by tank makers and a broken OEM-distributor-installer-homeowner chain; retrofit transponders destroy the economics.
insights.speaker: Luke Winston Almansar (Reservoir CEO)
insights.so_what: Factory-connected fleets (100% connected here) are the cheap way to build a VPP; connectivity at install is the moat.
insights.quote: if your devices aren't connected, you don't have a virtual power plant

insights.claim: Some Massachusetts municipal light plants have off-peak rates of 5 cents vs 50 cents on-peak (a 10x spread), letting a water heater act as a home thermal battery; major Massachusetts utilities lack such rates, and Reservoir is in talks with multiple utilities but has not enrolled customers in VPPs yet.
insights.speaker: Luke Winston Almansar (Reservoir CEO)
insights.so_what: Time-of-use rate design is the gating factor for water heater load-shifting value.

insights.claim: Flow sensing lets the company avoid enrolling households likely to run out of hot water in demand-response events, unlike thermostat programs where comfort loss drives opt-outs.
insights.speaker: Luke Winston Almansar (Reservoir CEO)
insights.so_what: Better targeting should lower VPP churn compared with HVAC-based programs.

insights.claim: The IRA federal tax credit for efficient water heaters ended at the end of last year, and the Trump administration is trying to rescind the DOE water heater efficiency standard slated for 2029 that the trade group expected to push heat pumps to ~50% of new units.
insights.speaker: David Roberts
insights.so_what: Two demand drivers are removed or at risk, so adoption must come from economics and service.

insights.claim: The CEO says he built the business to survive without incentives and that state incentives (Massachusetts, Maine, New England) have actually risen since the IRA credit ended, while pitching a 'better product' rather than mandates.
insights.speaker: Luke Winston Almansar (Reservoir CEO)
insights.so_what: State-level incentives partly backfill federal loss in blue-state markets that are also gas-heavy.
insights.quote: if you're building a business around incentives, that's not a business I really want to be in

insights.claim: Competing CO2-refrigerant split heat pump water heaters (AO Smith with Panasonic, similar to Sanden) work to -25 C-class cold, but Reservoir argues they cost more (Sanden systems over $10,000) and require outdoor pads and line penetrations, so it would not be cost competitive for most houses.
insights.speaker: Luke Winston Almansar (Reservoir CEO)
insights.so_what: Incumbent entry with a premium split system is a competitive risk, though the CEO claims it is price-disadvantaged; no AO Smith price had been published.

insights.claim: Management wants to extend from water heating to whole-home thermal management (space heating/cooling) with a goal of reaching 120 million US homes, noting that about 90% of homes are single-family and water heater install takes a morning versus an open-heart-surgery whole-home retrofit.
insights.speaker: Luke Winston Almansar (Reservoir CEO)
insights.so_what: Water heater is a beachhead; multifamily and HVAC are later, unproven expansions.
